label: Secretly Canadian
description: Jason Molina's debut as Songs: Ohia, nicknamed 'the Black Album' for its plain dark sleeve, is little more than his reverb-soaked tenor voice and a spare electric or tenor guitar, cut fast and self-distributed before Secretly Canadian picked it up. Song titles like 'Vanquisher' and 'Fortunate Man' sit over almost no percussion, just repeated, incantatory phrases about ghosts and Midwestern dark. It set the stark, haunted template Molina returned to for the rest of his career.
lineage: Grew out of the same lo-fi, DIY folk underground that produced Will Oldham's Palace records, and established the voice-and-guitar minimalism that every later Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co. record built from or reacted against.

label: Happy Go Lucky
description: Molina's second Songs: Ohia LP keeps the four-track hiss of the debut but adds a full, ramshackle band clattering behind him, giving songs like 'An Ace Unable to Change' a looser, more chaotic pulse. Parenthetical titles like '(Gambling Song)' and '(Trans Am)' hint at a private mythology that runs through the whole record. It is rougher and more obscure than the albums that followed, a transitional record between bedroom tape and full-band songwriter.
lineage: Bridges the stripped-down debut and the fuller-band Axxess & Ace, part of Molina's rapid early run of Secretly Canadian-adjacent releases out of the Bloomington/Chicago underground.
key_tracks: This Time Anything Finite at All

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Axxess & Ace tightens Molina's songwriting into something closer to conventional verse-chorus structure while keeping the hushed, echo-drenched production of his earliest work. 'Captain Badass' stretches out past seven minutes as a slow-burning centerpiece, while 'Love & Work' and 'Redhead' show a plainer, more direct kind of heartbreak song. It is often cited as the record where Molina's songwriting caught up with his atmosphere.
lineage: Continues the Secretly Canadian run that runs from Songs: Ohia's debut through The Lioness, tightening the songwriting that would fully bloom on Didn't It Rain and Magnolia Electric Co.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded near Glasgow with producer Andy Miller, Alasdair Roberts, and members of Arab Strap, The Lioness pairs Molina's voice with a chillier, more atmospheric backing than his American records, opening on the seven-minute drone of 'The Black Crow'. Songs like 'Lioness' and 'Tigress' move at a near-funereal pace, closer to Scottish folk-noir than to Americana. It is one of the clearest points of contact between the Songs: Ohia catalog and the Drag City/Will Oldham circle, via Roberts.
lineage: Made with Alasdair Roberts and Arab Strap's rhythm section in Scotland, linking the Songs: Ohia catalog directly to the UK folk underground that also produced Roberts's own records.
borderline_note: Recorded in Scotland with Alasdair Roberts; secondary_lanes flags the V2 (Drag City) overlap through Roberts and Will Oldham's circle.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded by Mike Mogis, Ghost Tropic is the slowest and most drone-like Songs: Ohia record, built from long, barely-moving pieces like the twelve-minute 'Not Just a Ghost's Heart' and the eleven-minute 'Incantation'. Molina's guitar and voice sit in wide, reverberant space rather than pushing toward a chorus, closer to American slowcore than to a folk or country record. It is the Songs: Ohia album most often cited as a bridge to the Low/Codeine slowcore lineage.
lineage: The most slowcore-indebted Songs: Ohia record, sitting between the folk-noir of The Lioness and the gospel-country turn of Didn't It Rain the following year.
borderline_note: Its drone-slow pacing overlaps with V12 slowcore; kept primary in V1 as a Molina-catalog essential.

album: Mi Sei Apparso Come Un Fantasma
label: Paper Cup
description: Recorded near Modena, Italy in 2000 with Molina's touring band of the Sullivan brothers, Jeff Panall and Jim Grabowski and released locally the following year, this live set captures the full-band version of Songs: Ohia mid-tour, reworking songs like 'Tigress' and 'Being in Love' from The Lioness alongside then-new, otherwise-untitled pieces. It is looser and more electric than the studio records of the same period, a document of the road band rather than a studio statement.
lineage: A snapshot of the touring band that also cut Ghost Tropic and Didn't It Rain, showing how the Songs: Ohia sound opened up once Molina had a full electric group behind him.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: A solo, mostly acoustic album sold at live shows in 2000 and long out of print, Protection Spells is one of Molina's least-heard records, closer in spirit to the stark debut than to the full-band records surrounding it. Songs like 'Trouble Will Find You' and 'The Moon Undoes It All' are recorded plainly, voice and guitar with little else. It survives mainly as a tour artifact rather than a widely distributed release, but its titles and mood run through Molina's later, more famous work.
lineage: A between-albums tour-only release from the same 2000 stretch that produced The Lioness and Ghost Tropic, showing the stripped-down solo mode Molina kept returning to between full-band records.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Released the same year as the Songs: Ohia debut, this early EP is spare, plainly recorded songs like 'Pass' and 'Defenders' that run only a minute or two apiece, closer to sketches than finished songs. It shares the debut's stark voice-and-guitar sound and dark, allusive titles. It is a minor, early document more than a destination record, useful mainly for hearing how quickly Molina was already writing and releasing material.
lineage: A same-year companion to the Songs: Ohia debut LP, part of the flood of early Secretly Canadian releases that established Molina's stark solo sound before the full band arrived.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded in Philadelphia with members of the bluegrass band Jim & Jennie & the Pinetops and named for a Mahalia Jackson song, Didn't It Rain trades Ghost Tropic's dense drone for a warmer, near-gospel small-group sound. The title track and 'Blue Factory Flame' stretch past seven and eight minutes on repeated, mantra-like phrases, while 'Two Blue Lights' offers a rare moment of brevity. Many fans and critics treat this as the true beginning of the Magnolia Electric Co. sound, one year before the name change.
lineage: The field guide's other suggested starting point alongside Magnolia Electric Co.; its gospel-tinged small-band sound is the direct bridge from the earlier solo Songs: Ohia records to the full-band Crazy Horse-scale group that followed.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Cut live in the studio with a full touring band, The Magnolia Electric Co. opens with the seven-minute 'Farewell Transmission' and never really lets up, trading Molina's earlier hushed folk for Crazy Horse-scale electric guitar, organ and drums. 'I've Been Riding with the Ghost' and 'Just Be Simple' pair big, ragged choruses with Molina's still-bleak lyrics about ghosts and highways. It is the record that gave the band its next name and its widest audience, and remains the most-cited entry point into the whole catalog.
lineage: Draws directly on Neil Young and Crazy Horse's guitar-heavy heartland rock and Molina's own heavy-metal roots, and gave its name to Magnolia Electric Co., the band Molina led for the next decade.
key_tracks: I've Been Riding with the Ghost
borderline_note: Crazy Horse-scale guitar sound overlaps with V20; kept primary in V1 as the catalog's best-known record.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Engineered by Mike Mogis, Pyramid Electric Co. strips everything back to Molina alone with voice, guitar and piano, the quietest record he made under his own name. The title track runs nearly nine minutes as a slow piano meditation, while 'Long Desert Train' closes the record on a similarly patient note. It is a deliberate come-down from the full-band Magnolia Electric Co. album released the year before, a private, unhurried companion piece.
lineage: A solo counterpart released the year after The Magnolia Electric Co., returning to the hushed, voice-and-instrument minimalism of the earliest Songs: Ohia records.

album: Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go
label: Secretly Canadian
description: Released the same year as Magnolia Electric Co.'s full-band Fading Trails, this sparse solo record leans on plain acoustic guitar and Molina's voice, with the title track closing things out at nearly seven minutes. Songs like 'It's Easier Now' and 'Alone With the Owl' keep the arrangements minimal so the lyrics about isolation and endurance carry the weight. It is one of the most purely singer-songwriter entries in Molina's catalog, closer to the folk end of his sound than to the band's rock side.
lineage: Continues the solo, stripped-down thread running from Pyramid Electric Co. through Molina's later work, released as a quiet counterweight to the same year's full-band Fading Trails.
key_tracks: Let Me Go Let Me Go Let Me Go

label: Graveface Records
description: An eight-song, twenty-two-minute set released during Molina's illness, Autumn Bird Songs is brief, plainly recorded songs like 'Heart My Heart' and 'The Harvest Law' that feel closer to sketches than to a full statement. It is quieter and more fragile than his earlier work, released on Graveface rather than his usual home at Secretly Canadian. For a small, committed audience it is one of the last pieces of new music Molina put out in his lifetime.
lineage: One of Molina's final releases before his 2013 death, extending the hushed solo-acoustic mode of Pyramid Electric Co. and Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go into a briefer, more fragile form.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded in the 2000s but shelved until after Molina's 2013 death, Eight Gates was assembled and released by Secretly Canadian in 2020 as a posthumous studio album. Opener 'Whisper Away' and 'Shadow Answers the Wall' sit in the same hushed, piano-and-guitar territory as Pyramid Electric Co., by turns unfinished-sounding and quietly devastating. It gave fans a final, previously unheard chapter of Molina's writing, released under his own name seven years after he died.
lineage: A posthumous release of 2000s-era Molina recordings, closing out the catalog begun with Songs: Ohia's 1997 debut and continued through his solo and Magnolia Electric Co. work.
borderline_note: Posthumous 2020 release of earlier recordings; logged under its release year per lane instructions.
